sample.method: GitHub code search for each of the three files at a project root (up to the first 300 results per file, forks and the maintainer's own repositories left out), then a seeded random draw from the results, with each of the three files fetched from every drawn repository.

notes: Every alert matched the labelling rule as written. 4 of them are right only by the rule's wording and look harmless in context: a `NODE_OPTIONS` value that only sets a memory limit (ENDPOINT), two `npx` launches of tools that are usually installed in the project (MCP), and a plain `sh -c "cd … && exec …"` launch (MCP). These are candidates for narrowing the rules, not counted as false alarms.
Only config files were fetched, so DENY (needs a secrets file), SKILL (needs scripts) and DRIFT (needs a baseline) can't fire here. HOOK and HTTPHOOK could fire but raised no alerts in this sample.
Search results are ranked by GitHub, not random, and repositories that commit these files may differ from those that keep them local. Treat the sample as indicative, not representative.
Secret alerts were labelled from the masked output only (key name and value length). The values were never opened.

Seen while labelling, not counted: allow rules for package managers with any arguments (`npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `pip`, `uv`) raise no alert, though `npm exec`, `pnpm dlx` and `uv run` can run packages. The labelling rule doesn't settle whether they should.
